title: What has changed since the OBR's March 2026 forecast
intro: The OBR's March forecast is your baseline. Six months on, markets and forecasters have moved. Confirm its assumptions or replace them with your own.

readings.title: 10-year gilt yield

obr.label: Market expectations in the 10 working days to 22 January 2026

source.quote: Medium-term forecasts for the official Bank rate, annual average, per cent.

alternatives.note: These rows are for the official Bank Rate, not gilt yields. No forecaster in the comparison publishes a gilt yield, so the published range for this slider is a Bank Rate range, while your adviser reads the 10-year gilt yield above. The slider moves both together.

against.label: OBR March 2026, as printed by the Treasury alongside the forecasters

lowest.label: Lowest of the forecasts in the comparison

highest.label: Highest of the forecasts in the comparison

readings.text: The OBR conditioned its March forecast on 10-year gilt yields of 4.5%. They have since risen to about 5.35%. The OBR's own sensitivity puts a sustained 1 percentage point rise in Bank Rate and gilt yields at about £15 billion of extra borrowing by 2030-31, so this is the largest single change since March.

readings.title: Bank Rate
readings.text: Bank Rate is 3.75%, close to the average the OBR assumed. The rates slider moves Bank Rate and gilt yields together, so the advisers set it from the gilt yield gap.

readings.title: Real GDP growth

latest.label: Average of independent medium-term forecasts, August 2026

suggestion.rationale: Independent forecasters expect weaker real growth than the OBR from 2027 (about 0.2 percentage points a year less on average) but higher inflation (about 0.3 points more). Receipts follow nominal GDP, where the two roughly cancel, so the advisers suggest leaving the growth slider on the OBR path and treating the weaker real outlook as a risk.

readings.text: Independent forecasters agree with the OBR for 2026 but expect growth of 1.2% rather than 1.6% in 2027 and 1.4% rather than 1.6% in 2028. Weaker real growth is partly offset for the public finances by higher inflation, which raises cash receipts.

readings.title: CPI inflation

latest.label: Average of the forecasts the Treasury received in August 2026

readings.text: Independent forecasters expect CPI inflation of 3.1% this year and 2.7% next, against the OBR's 2.3% and 2.0%. Higher inflation raises both receipts and spending; only the RPI channel, which drives index-linked debt interest, has a slider here.

readings.title: CPI inflation, latest month
readings.text: CPI inflation was 2.9% in the year to July 2026, above the OBR's 2.3% for 2026 as a whole.

alternatives.note: The Treasury prints the OBR’s own RPI row in this table year by year; the comparison above uses the OBR’s stated average for 2027 to 2029, so the two differ slightly for those years. The range is measured against the row printed beside it.

against.label: OBR March 2026, as printed by the Treasury alongside the forecasters

lowest.label: Lowest of the forecasts in the comparison

highest.label: Highest of the forecasts in the comparison

readings.text: RPI inflation sets the interest on index-linked gilts: the OBR's sensitivity puts 1 percentage point on RPI at about £11 billion of extra borrowing by 2030-31. Independent forecasters see RPI about half a point higher than the OBR over the next five years; the outturn was 3.2% in July 2026.

readings.title: Borrowing (PSNB)

latest.label: Average of independent medium-term forecasts, August 2026

readings.text: Independent forecasters expect borrowing above the OBR's March path in every year, by £27 billion in 2029-30. The sliders capture the interest-rate and inflation parts of that gap, not all of it.

readings.title: Borrowing so far in 2026-27

obr.label: OBR March 2026 monthly profile, April to July (outturn less the £2.3 billion overshoot reported by the ONS)

readings.text: Borrowing in the first four months of 2026-27 was £56.7 billion, £2.3 billion above the OBR's profile, with a small surplus in July.

scenarios.title: Keep the March baseline
scenarios.headline: The OBR’s own central forecast, left exactly as it was. The figures your Budget will be judged on.

rationale.text: This is the forecast your Budget will be judged against until the OBR publishes a new one on 28 October. The OBR’s own warning about it: a central forecast is the middle of a range of possible outcomes, with a low probability of the outcome being very close to the central estimate.
Six months of market moves and forecaster revisions sit outside it. The other three cards each apply one stated rule to published figures to close part of that gap.

scenarios.title: Your Chief Economic Adviser’s view
scenarios.headline: Today’s readings, not a forecast: each slider moved by the gap between the latest figure and the OBR’s.

rationale.text: Gilt yields are the large change. The OBR conditioned March on 10-year yields of 4.5%; they closed at 5.35% on 11 September. The OBR’s sensitivity puts a sustained point on rates at about £15 billion of borrowing by 2030-31.
RPI runs about half a point above the OBR’s path on the average of independent forecasts, which is what sets the interest on index-linked gilts.

Growth stays on the OBR’s path: forecasters see weaker real growth but higher inflation, and receipts follow nominal GDP, where the two roughly cancel. The weaker real outlook is a risk your adviser leaves on the table rather than a number.

scenarios.title: An optimistic analyst
scenarios.headline: The kindest figure published anywhere for each assumption — whoever published it, and whichever table it sits in.

rationale.text: Rates do the work. The lowest Bank Rate path in the Treasury’s comparison runs about 0.6 points a year below the OBR’s, falling to 2.59% by 2030 where the OBR has 3.89%. Borrowing gets cheaper than the March forecast assumed, and nothing else published is kinder.

But there is no optimistic case on inflation. The lowest published RPI path is within 0.2 points of the OBR’s, so the rule rounds it to nothing: not one forecaster in the comparison sees RPI materially below the OBR, and on the quarterly basis the lowest 2026 forecast sits above it, not below.

Growth stays on the OBR’s path, because there is no published figure to move it to. The comparison gives no medium-term range for nominal GDP, and adding its highest real growth to its highest GDP deflator would splice together different institutions into a path nobody published.

scenarios.title: A pessimistic analyst
scenarios.headline: The cruellest figure published anywhere for each assumption. An envelope, not one forecaster’s view.

rationale.text: The gloomiest figure for interest rates is not a forecast at all. None of the sixteen forecasters in the comparison publishes a gilt yield — their range is for Bank Rate, and its top is milder than the market. So this card takes today’s 10-year gilt yield, 5.35% against the 4.5% the OBR assumed, the same figure your adviser reads. Gilt yields, not Bank Rate, are what drive debt interest.

Inflation is where this parts company with your adviser. The highest published RPI path runs more than a point a year above the OBR’s, against the half point the average of forecasts gives, and the OBR’s own sensitivity puts a point on RPI at about £11 billion of extra borrowing by 2030-31, mostly through index-linked gilts.

Growth stays on the OBR’s path, because there is no published figure to move it to. The comparison gives no medium-term range for nominal GDP, and adding its highest real growth to its highest GDP deflator would splice together different institutions into a path nobody published.

No single analyst holds this whole view. Each cell in the comparison’s highest row can come from a different institution, and the rates figure is a market reading rather than a forecast. It is the outer edge of what has been published, which is why it is a card and not a forecast.
